title: Deconsolidation: Accounting for a Subsidiary You Sell or Close
summary: Deconsolidation accounting under ASC 810-10-40: when control ends, how the gain or loss is computed, and what the final close on the entity has to cover.
body_markdown:
## When a Parent Has to Deconsolidate


Deconsolidation accounting starts on the date the parent stops having a controlling financial interest, not on the closing date in the purchase agreement. ASC 810-10-40-4 fixes the trigger at loss of control, which is how a signing in one quarter and a control transfer in the next land in two different reporting periods. That date is the first thing indinero’s accounting team pins down when a group takes an entity out of consolidation, because it decides which period carries the gain.


Everything else follows from it.


This page is the exit side.[Post-acquisition accounting integration](https://www.indinero.com/blog/post-acquisition-accounting-integration/) is the mirror image, same ledger, opposite direction.


Check scope first. The ASC 810-10-40 loss of control model, scoped at ASC 810-10-40-3A, covers a subsidiary or asset group that is a business or a nonprofit activity. A single-asset LLC holding nothing but a note receivable often isn’t a business, which routes the exit into ASC 610-20 or ASC 860 instead.


### The events that end control


The national firms’ consolidation guides place the enumerated fact patterns at ASC 810-10-55-4A, and the list runs wider than “we sold it.”


- **A sale that drops the interest below control.** 100 percent to 45 percent is a deconsolidation. 100 percent to 80 percent isn’t, it’s an equity transaction under ASC 810-10-45-23 with no gain.
- **Expiry of a contractual control right.** Control that came from a management agreement or a board-appointment right rather than from votes can simply lapse.
- **Dilution by a subsidiary share issuance.** The parent writes no check and the subsidiary still leaves the group. Subsidiary-level investor rounds are the usual cause.
- **Control passing to a government, court, administrator, or regulator.** Bankruptcy, receivership, or a liquidator substitutes someone else’s control for the parent’s.


Add dissolution to the practical list. Control ends at wind-down even though nobody acquired the entity.


### Two statements, two cut-offs


The consolidated income statement keeps the subsidiary line by line through the deconsolidation date, with the NCI share attributed through that date. Prior periods aren’t restated. At period end the balance sheet shows none of its assets or liabilities, only the consideration received and any retained investment on one line.


So a subsidiary sold on November 12 contributes about ten and a half months of operations to a December 31 income statement and nothing to the December 31 balance sheet. That asymmetry is what reviewers question first, which is why an exit belongs inside the[multi-entity consolidation process](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-consolidation-process/) and not bolted onto year end.


## Calculating the Gain or Loss on Deconsolidation


The gain or loss on deconsolidation is measured under ASC 810-10-40-5 as a four-component aggregate, computed at the control date. Run the components separately and don’t net until all four are on the schedule. The accounting for the sale of a subsidiary effected as a spin-off or split-off, a nonreciprocal transfer to owners, goes to ASC 845 instead.


### Component by component


- **(a)(1) Consideration received, at fair value.** Cash, any note or equity instrument, and contingent consideration. An earnout is measured at the deconsolidation date and remeasured afterward outside the gain.
- **(a)(2) Any retained noncontrolling investment, at fair value.** Not carried over at book. It drops an unrealized amount into net income beside the realized piece.
- **(a)(3) Carrying amount of any noncontrolling interest.** Including the AOCI attributable to that NCI, which reduces what the parent gives up.
- **(b) Carrying amount of the former subsidiary’s assets and liabilities.** At consolidated carrying amounts on the control date, with goodwill allocated from the reporting unit that included it. Intercompany is already eliminated inside those numbers.


### The AOCI and translation reclassification


This step sits in a different paragraph from the formula, which is why it gets missed. ASC 810-10-40-4A, added by ASU 2013-05, requires the parent to derecognize the equity components related to the subsidiary, including any noncontrolling interest and any amounts previously recognized in accumulated other comprehensive income. Where the entity is a foreign entity, or the transaction is the complete or substantially complete liquidation of the foreign entity in which it resides, the reclassified AOCI includes the foreign currency translation adjustment.


Four ASC 830 paragraphs carry the detail. ASC 830-30-40-1 releases the translation adjustment into the gain on sale or liquidation. ASC 830-30-40-1A makes a loss of controlling financial interest a sale, so control loss recycles CTA even with a stake retained. ASC 830-30-40-2 releases a pro rata portion on a partial sale. ASC 830-30-40-3 is the sharp edge: a derecognition inside a foreign entity releases nothing unless it is that entity’s complete or substantially complete liquidation. Practice, not the standard, puts “substantially complete” at roughly 90 percent of net assets. The mechanics belong to[foreign subsidiary accounting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/foreign-subsidiary-accounting/) .


### A worked computation


A parent sells its entire 80 percent interest for $9,000,000 cash. Consolidated net assets are $6,000,000, NCI carries at $1,400,000, and parent AOCI holds a cumulative translation debit of $500,000.


Component ASC reference Amount


Consideration received 810-10-40-5(a)(1) $9,000,000


Retained noncontrolling investment 810-10-40-5(a)(2) $0


Noncontrolling interest derecognized 810-10-40-5(a)(3) $1,400,000


Net assets derecognized 810-10-40-5(b) ($6,000,000)


Translation adjustment reclassified 810-10-40-4A, 830-30-40-1 ($500,000)


**Gain on deconsolidation** **$3,900,000**


The entry credits AOCI to clear the translation debit, which reduces the gain. A translation credit would increase it. The sale price never moved.


### Where the gain is presented, and what you disclose


Discontinued operations reporting isn’t automatic. ASC 205-20-45-1B requires the disposal of a component, or group of components, to represent a strategic shift with a major effect on operations and financial results. Neither term is defined, and the ASC 205-20-55 illustrations sit around 15 percent of revenues and 20 percent of assets. Clear the bar and the results and the disposal gain move to discontinued operations net of tax, with comparatives reclassified. Miss it and the gain stays in continuing operations, caption disclosed under ASC 810-10-50-1B(c).


ASC 810-10-50-1B(a) through (h) covers the disclosures: the gain, the remeasurement portion, the caption, the valuation technique and its inputs, continuing involvement, and related-party status before and after. A seller note or a transition services agreement counts as continuing involvement. That’s the part private groups skip.


## What Happens to a Stake You Keep


A retained stake is remeasured to fair value at the deconsolidation date, and that fair value becomes the opening carrying amount of the new investment. The book value of the interest you kept stops mattering on the control date.


Where it lands depends on influence. If the retained interest conveys significant influence, it goes to the equity method under ASC 323, with the ASC 810-10-40-5 fair value as the opening basis and a basis difference against the proportionate share of the investee’s underlying net assets to track from then on. The significant-influence test and the equity method mechanics belong to[equity method vs consolidation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/equity-method-vs-consolidation/) . With no significant influence, the stake is an ASC 321 equity security. A private former subsidiary rarely has a readily determinable fair value, so a nonpublic holder may elect the ASC 321-10-35-2 measurement alternative and carry it at cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for an identical or similar investment of the same issuer.


Two practical notes. The price paid for the block you sold is evidence of fair value, not an answer, because a controlling block often prices at a premium and grossing that price up overstates a minority stake. And the retained investment shows up as a single line at period end. The former subsidiary’s gross assets and liabilities don’t come back.


## The Final Close on an Entity Being Wound Down


The question controllers actually ask is how to close down a subsidiary, not how to book the entry. The GAAP entry is one line in the ledger. The technical literature stops there.


The entity close is a project.


### Settle the intercompany before you dissolve


Do this first, because a dissolved entity can’t sign anything or be invoiced. Reconcile every intercompany account to the counterparty’s balance, since mismatched intercompany is the most common reason a close like this slips. Then decide each balance. Settle in cash, capitalize the payable into the subsidiary’s equity, forgive it, or distribute it, with a resolution dated before dissolution.


Those balances were already eliminated in consolidation, so the write-off produces no consolidated gain. It isn’t free at the entity level. A forgiven payable can create cancellation-of-indebtedness income in the subsidiary and a bad debt question for the lender entity. If the subsidiary is an insolvent corporation, IRC section 332 non-recognition doesn’t apply and the parent may instead have a worthless security deduction under section 165(g). Decide that before dissolution, not after.


### Final federal returns, payroll, and the final-return box


The IRS guidance on[closing a business](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/closing-a-business) sets the list. A partnership or multi-member LLC files Form 1065 with the final return box checked and the final K-1 box checked on every Schedule K-1. A C corporation files Form 1120 and an S corporation files Form 1120-S, both marking the final return. A corporation that adopts a resolution or plan to dissolve, or to liquidate any of its stock, files Form 966.


Payroll closes separately. File Form 941 or 944 for the quarter final wages were paid, with the closure box checked, and Form 940 for that year with box “d” checked. Issue Forms W-2 with the W-3 transmittal, and Form 1099-NEC with Form 1096 for contractors paid $600 or more.


The final-return box isn’t cosmetic. It’s the instruction that closes the IRS filing account. Leave it unchecked and the entity stays an expected filer, generating notices to an address nobody monitors.[Business tax services](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) is where those final returns get handled.


### State dissolution and withdrawal, so franchise tax stops


Franchise tax is an existence tax in most states, not an activity tax. It accrues because the entity is still on the register, and that’s where groups lose real money for years after an entity goes dark.


- **Delaware.** The Division of Corporations states that taxes continue to accrue until a filing is received that officially terminates the corporation’s existence in the state.
- **California.** FTB Publication 1038 requires both steps. File the final return with the Final Return box checked, then file the dissolution, surrender, or cancellation documents with the Secretary of State within 12 months of that return’s filing date. Miss either and the $800 minimum franchise tax keeps accruing.
- **Texas.** A final franchise tax report is due 60 days after the entity ceased doing business there. Termination or withdrawal requires a Comptroller certificate of account status filed with the Secretary of State.


Run the same sequence in every state, not just the state of formation. A certificate of withdrawal everywhere the entity was foreign-qualified. Closed sales tax permits and closed withholding and unemployment accounts, because an open account generates a filing obligation on its own.


### Close the bank account last, then keep the records


Not first. The entity still has to pay final tax bills, collect the last receipts, fund the final payroll deposit, and clear checks cut before the wind-down. Keep one account open, with one authorized signer, until every final return is accepted and every refund is received.


Close it last.


On records, the IRS period of limitations is 3 years by default, 6 years where omitted income exceeds 25 percent of reported gross income, and 7 years where a worthless securities or bad debt claim was filed. A wound-down subsidiary usually involves one of those claims, so plan on 7 years. Keep the dissolution certificates, the plan of liquidation, the intercompany resolutions, and the deconsolidation workpaper with the ASC 810-10-40-5 computation. Assign one named owner at the parent.


## Common Pitfalls


Each of these is an observed audit adjustment or restatement pattern, not a hypothetical.


1. **Deconsolidating on the legal closing date.** A regulatory consent, a share escrow, or a transition period where the seller still appoints the board splits the closing date from the control date, which puts the gain in the wrong period.
2. **Forgetting to recycle the translation adjustment.** The CTA sits in equity and nobody looks at it during a close, even though ASC 810-10-40-4A and ASC 830-30-40-1 require it. The mirror error is releasing CTA on a disposal inside a foreign entity without the substantially complete liquidation ASC 830-30-40-3 demands.
3. **Leaving an intercompany receivable on a surviving entity’s books.** It was eliminated in consolidation, so the consolidated statements look clean and the problem hides. The standalone balance sheet now carries a receivable from a dissolved counterparty, which fails any entity-level audit or lender certificate.
4. **Dissolving in the state of formation only.** Delaware accrues tax until a terminating document is filed, California needs both the final return and the Secretary of State filing, and Texas needs a Comptroller certificate first. Miss one registration and the tax, penalties, and interest run for years.
5. **Assuming a retained stake carries over at book value.** ASC 810-10-40-5(a)(2) measures it at fair value through net income. Carrying it at book understates the gain and starts the equity method on a wrong basis.
6. **Treating a common-control transfer as a sale.** Moving a subsidiary to another company under the same ultimate owner isn’t a deconsolidation at fair value. ASC 805-50-30-5 requires carryover basis at the transferring entity’s carrying amounts, any difference against consideration is an equity transaction rather than income, and ASC 805-50-45-2 through 45-5 govern the retrospective presentation. See[combined financial statements under common control](https://www.indinero.com/blog/combined-financial-statements-common-control/) .

## Frequently asked questions


Seven questions come up on almost every exit, and most of them are about dates, presentation, and what keeps filing after the lights go out. Short answers below. The ASC references behind each one sit in the sections above.


### What date does a subsidiary actually come off the consolidated balance sheet?


A subsidiary leaves the consolidated balance sheet on the date the parent loses a controlling financial interest, which ASC 810-10-40-4 sets as the trigger. That isn’t the legal closing date and it isn’t period end, because a regulatory consent, a share escrow, or a seller who still appoints the board can push control past signing. A deal signed in one quarter can deconsolidate in the next, so the control date decides which period carries the gain.


### Does the subsidiary’s income still appear in the consolidated P&L for the year it leaves?


Yes, the subsidiary’s results stay in the consolidated income statement through the deconsolidation date, with the noncontrolling interest share attributed through that same date. At period end, though, none of its assets or liabilities appear on the consolidated balance sheet, and prior periods aren’t restated. A subsidiary sold on November 12 contributes roughly ten and a half months of operations to a December 31 income statement and nothing to the December 31 balance sheet.


### Is a transfer of a subsidiary to another company we own also a deconsolidation?


No, moving a subsidiary to another entity under the same ultimate owner is a common-control transfer rather than a deconsolidation at fair value. ASC 805-50-30-5 requires carryover basis at the transferring entity’s carrying amounts, so the consolidated group recognizes no gain and any difference against consideration runs through equity. This is the most commonly misbooked exit, because the legal paperwork looks exactly like a third-party sale.


### Does the sale of a subsidiary have to be reported as a discontinued operation?


No, a sale only becomes a discontinued operation if the disposal represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations and financial results. ASC 205-20-45-1B sets that threshold and defines neither term, so the codification illustrations around 15 percent of revenues and 20 percent of assets carry the judgment. Clear the bar and the results and the gain move net of tax with comparatives reclassified, otherwise the gain stays in continuing operations with the caption disclosed.


### Do we keep filing for an entity after it stops operating?


Yes, a wound-down entity keeps filing until final federal and state returns are submitted with the final-return box checked and state registrations are closed. Payroll closes separately with a final Form 941 or 944, Form 940, Forms W-2, and Form 1099-NEC, and a dissolving corporation also files Form 966. File dissolution or withdrawal documents in every state the entity was registered in, or franchise tax keeps accruing. In a bundled indinero engagement, the final returns and the deconsolidation entry sit with one team instead of three vendors.


### How is a retained minority stake measured once control is lost?


A retained minority stake is remeasured to fair value at the date control is lost, and that fair value becomes its opening carrying amount. Book value stops mattering on the control date, and the remeasurement runs through net income beside any realized gain. Significant influence puts the investment on the equity method under ASC 323, while no significant influence makes it an ASC 321 equity security. Indinero’s CPA-led team documents the fair value support at the control date instead of reconstructing it a year later for an auditor.


### What records should the group keep after an entity is dissolved?


Keep the dissolved entity’s tax returns, dissolution certificates, intercompany resolutions, and the deconsolidation workpaper for as long as the IRS limitations period runs. That period is 3 years by default, 6 years when omitted income exceeds 25 percent of reported gross income, and 7 years when a worthless securities or bad debt claim was filed. A wound-down subsidiary usually involves one of those claims, so plan on 7 years and give one named owner at the parent custody of the file.
